items.title: Weimar Germany had a 'golden' decade — but it was built on US loans
items.claim: Why did Weimar's relative stability (1924-1929) collapse?

options.text: The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured reparations with US loans; the Wall Street Crash (October 1929) collapsed lending; Stresemann had died in October 1929; unemployment hit 6 million by 1932
The British naval blockade resumed in 1927

items.reveal:
The Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929) refinanced German reparations through US bank loans. Germany used the loans for infrastructure, social housing and reparations payments — a circular flow.

Gustav Stresemann's diplomacy (Locarno 1925, German League membership 1926) normalised relations with the West. He died on 3 October 1929, three weeks before the Wall Street Crash.

When US loans dried up, German banks failed (Danatbank, July 1931); unemployment soared; the Nazis went from 12 seats (1928) to 230 seats (July 1932), becoming the largest party.
items.why: Weimar's 'collapse' was not inevitable but was structurally vulnerable. The Crash was an external shock that destroyed a recovery dependent on foreign credit — a useful case in how interconnected economies fail.

items.title: Domesday Book was completed in around a year
items.claim: How quickly was Domesday Book compiled?

options.text: Commissioned by William I at Christmas 1085, the survey of around 13,000 places was largely completed within a year, with the final two-volume Great Domesday and Little Domesday produced by 1086

items.reveal:
Commissioners visited each shire, taking sworn testimony from jury panels of local landholders. The survey recorded who held land before and after 1066, the value, the population, the resources (ploughs, mills, fishponds, pasture).

The survey was unprecedented in medieval Europe in its speed and detail. The name 'Domesday' (judgment day) was applied by users by around 1100 — they could not appeal against its findings, as they could not appeal against the Last Judgment.

The manuscripts (Great Domesday for most of England, Little Domesday for Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex) survive at The National Archives in Kew.
items.why: Medieval government was capable of administrative effort that would not be matched in Europe for centuries. Domesday's speed and accuracy is one of the strongest counters to the 'Dark Ages' frame.

items.title: The Dissolution of the Monasteries was a wealth transfer
items.claim: Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries (1536-1541). How much was at stake financially?

options.text: A symbolic amount; most monasteries were poor
The monasteries owned around a quarter of the cultivated land in England; their dissolution transferred wealth equivalent to several times the crown's annual income
The proceeds were used to found grammar schools across the country
Only the buildings were seized; lands remained in religious hands

items.reveal:
Thomas Cromwell's Valor Ecclesiasticus (1535) surveyed monastic incomes — around £160,000 a year, against royal ordinary revenue of about £100,000. The Court of Augmentations was created to handle the proceeds.

Much of the land was sold below market to gentry buyers, creating a new class with a stake in keeping the Reformation. Cathedrals like Glastonbury were destroyed; libraries were dispersed (John Leland's lament). The wealth was largely spent on war with France within a decade.
items.why: The break with Rome was about Anne Boleyn and the king's conscience — but it was also the biggest fiscal opportunity an English king had had since the Conquest. Mixed motives, both real.
